claim: The unfolded protein response (UPR) is a key signaling system that regulates protein homeostasis within the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: The unfolded protein response (UPR) is a key signaling system that regulates protein homeostasis within the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the UPR system.

claim: The response is induced when there is an accumulation of misfolded protein—due to increase in protein load or aberrant protein folding.
source: The response is induced when there is an accumulation of misfolded protein—due to increase in protein load or aberrant protein folding, which results in activation of a cellular program that aims to restore correctly folded protein levels, in order to ensure a properly functioning ER (Schneider and Bertolotti, 2015; Wang and Kaufman, 2016; Hetz and Papa, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: An allosteric model for UPR induction was previously reported by Carrara et al., 2015.
source: We have previously reported an allosteric model for UPR induction (Carrara et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The allosteric model was based on the observation that an interaction between the luminal domain (LD) of IRE1 and the ATPase domain of BiP dissociates upon the binding of CH1 misfolded protein to the canonical BiP substrate-binding domain.
source: Our model was based on the observation that a interaction between the luminal domain (LD) of the key UPR protein, IRE1, and the ATPase domain of BiP, an ER Hsp70 chaperone, dissociates upon the binding of CH1 misfolded protein to the canonical BiP substrate-binding domain.
evidence: Describes the basis of the previously reported model.

claim: A pull-down assay was previously utilized to qualitatively measure noncanonical dissociation.
source: To observe this important step, we utilized a pull-down assay that qualitatively measured noncanonical dissociation (Carrara et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to prior methodology used by the authors.

claim: A Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) UPR induction assay was developed that quantifies the association and subsequent dissociation of IRE1 LD with BiP upon addition of misfolded protein.
source: In the present study, we developed a Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) UPR induction assay that quantifies the association and subsequent dissociation of IRE1 LD with BiP, upon addition of misfolded protein.
evidence: Describes the new experimental technique developed in this study.

claim: The new experimental technique reconstitutes in vitro the most crucial mechanistic step in UPR signaling, namely, the detection of misfolded protein and UPR induction.
source: This new experimental technique reconstitutes in vitro the most crucial mechanistic step in UPR signaling, namely, the detection of misfolded protein and UPR induction.
evidence: Interpretation of the significance of the developed assay.

claim: An interaction between the N-terminal ATPase domain of BiP and IRE1 LD was previously measured with Kd = 1.33 μM.
source: As we have previously measured an interaction between the N-terminal ATPase domain of BiP and IRE1 LD (Kd = 1.33 μM), and our pull-down assays utilized an N-terminus-positioned affinity tag that had no impact on interaction (Carrara et al., 2015), we attached fluorescent proteins to the N-terminus of both constructs, with YFP connected via short linker to BiP, upstream of the ATPase domain; and similarly, CFP to IRE1 LD (Figure 1A).
evidence: Reference to prior measurement with specific Kd value.

claim: N-terminus-positioned affinity tags had no impact on the interaction between BiP and IRE1 LD.
source: As we have previously measured an interaction between the N-terminal ATPase domain of BiP and IRE1 LD (Kd = 1.33 μM), and our pull-down assays utilized an N-terminus-positioned affinity tag that had no impact on interaction (Carrara et al., 2015), we attached fluorescent proteins to the N-terminus of both constructs, with YFP connected via short linker to BiP, upstream of the ATPase domain; and similarly, CFP to IRE1 LD (Figure 1A).
evidence: Reference to prior experimental observation.

claim: YFP was connected via short linker to BiP, upstream of the ATPase domain.
source: we attached fluorescent proteins to the N-terminus of both constructs, with YFP connected via short linker to BiP, upstream of the ATPase domain; and similarly, CFP to IRE1 LD (Figure 1A).
evidence: Describes the construct design used in the study, also shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CFP was attached to the N-terminus of IRE1 LD.
source: we attached fluorescent proteins to the N-terminus of both constructs, with YFP connected via short linker to BiP, upstream of the ATPase domain; and similarly, CFP to IRE1 LD (Figure 1A).
evidence: Describes the construct design used in the study, also shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CFP-IRE1 LD is excited at 430 nm with a bandwidth of 10 nm.
source: CFP-IRE1 LD will be excited at 430 nm with a bandwidth of 10 nm (430–10 nm), and upon excitement it will emit radiation at the longer wavelength of 480–10 nm.
evidence: Describes the experimental parameters for FRET measurement, also illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Upon excitation, CFP-IRE1 LD emits radiation at 480 nm with a bandwidth of 10 nm.
source: CFP-IRE1 LD will be excited at 430 nm with a bandwidth of 10 nm (430–10 nm), and upon excitement it will emit radiation at the longer wavelength of 480–10 nm.
evidence: Describes the emission properties of CFP, also illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: When YFP-BiP is added, IRE1 LD interacts with BiP via its ATPase domain, bringing YFP in close proximity to CFP, resulting in FRET between the fluorescent proteins and an emission at 530 nm.
source: When YFP-BiP is added, IRE1 LD should interact with BiP via its ATPase domain, bringing YFP in close proximity to CFP, resulting in FRET between the fluorescent proteins and an emission at 530–10 nm.
evidence: Describes the expected mechanism of FRET signal generation, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Dissociation of the IRE1-BiP complex with loss of FRET signal occurs upon addition of misfolded protein, which binds to BiP substrate-binding domain (SBD) to cause conformational change.
source: Dissociation of the complex—with loss of FRET signal—should occur upon addition of misfolded protein, which will bind to BiP substrate-binding domain (SBD) to cause conformational change.
evidence: Describes the predicted outcome of adding misfolded protein, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The ratio of 530-10 nm/480-10 nm is used to measure FRET signal output.
source: The ratio of 530-10 nm/480-10 nm will be used to measure FRET signal output.
evidence: Describes the measurement method for FRET, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The FRET ratio for CFP-IRE1 LD with YFP-BiP is approximately 0.62.
source: Upon excitation, we observed a FRET ratio (530-10 nm/480-10nm) of ~0.62 for CFP-IRE1 LD with YFP-BiP.
evidence: Experimental measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The FRET ratio for non-binding controls is approximately 0.34.
source: For our non-binding controls, we measured a FRET ratio of ~0.34 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The FRET ratio for CFP-IRE1 LD with YFP-BiP is almost doubled compared to non-binding controls.
source: The data show an almost doubling of the FRET ratio for CFP-IRE1 LD with YFP-BiP when compared to non-binding controls.
evidence: Comparison of experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The almost doubling of FRET ratio represents a significant FRET signal between the two fluorescent proteins.
source: This represents a significant FRET signal between the two fluorescent proteins (Pollok and Heim, 1999) that was easily reproducible.
evidence: Interpretation of the data with citation to FRET methodology literature.

claim: The FRET signal indicates a direct interaction between the IRE1 LD and the BiP ATPase domain that can be quantifiably measured.
source: Moreover, it indicates a direct interaction between the IRE1 LD and the BiP ATPase domain that we can quantifiably measure.
evidence: Interpretation of the FRET data.

claim: Misfolded protein CH1 binds to the canonical SBP of BiP and effects dissociation of BiP from IRE1 LD.
source: We have previously demonstrated that misfolded protein, CH1, binds to the canonical SBP of BiP, and effects dissociation of BiP from IRE1 LD.
evidence: Reference to prior experimental findings.

claim: Addition of 10-fold molar excess of CH1 to CFP-IRE1 LD and YFP-BiP reduced the FRET signal to approximately 4%.
source: Upon addition of CH1, the FRET signal was reduced to ~4% (Figure 1D), clearly indicating that the binding of CH1 misfolded protein to the canonical BiP SBD caused the dissociation of the BiP ATPase domain from the IRE1 LD.
evidence: Experimental measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The binding of CH1 misfolded protein to the canonical BiP SBD caused the dissociation of the BiP ATPase domain from the IRE1 LD.
source: Upon addition of CH1, the FRET signal was reduced to ~4% (Figure 1D), clearly indicating that the binding of CH1 misfolded protein to the canonical BiP SBD caused the dissociation of the BiP ATPase domain from the IRE1 LD.
evidence: Interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The addition of CH1 reduced the FRET signal in a dose-dependent fashion with an inhibition constant Ki = 0.51 ± 0.01 μM.
source: We found that the addition of CH1 reduced the FRET signal in a dose-dependent fashion (inhibition constant Ki = 0.51 ± 0.01 μM) (Figure 2), with 10-fold molar excess reducing the FRET signal to almost non-binding control levels.
evidence: Experimental measurement with dose-response analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: 10-fold molar excess of CH1 was sufficient for almost complete inhibition of FRET signal.
source: This suggests that a 10-fold molar excess of CH1 was sufficient for almost complete inhibition of FRET signal.
evidence: Interpretation of dose-response data from Figure 2.

claim: At 300 μM CH1, a 10-fold molar excess over both CFP-IRE1 LD and YFP-BiP, the FRET signal was almost completely inhibited.
source: At 300 μM CH1, a 10-fold molar excess over both CFP-IRE1 LD and YFP-BiP, the signal was almost completely inhibited.
evidence: Experimental observation from dose-response curve shown in Figure 2.

claim: The IC50 of CH1 for inhibiting the IRE1-BiP interaction is 12.3 ± 1.3 μM.
source: Fitting an exponential (two phase association, r2 = 0.98) curve to data gave an IC50 of 12.3 ± 1.3 μM, the amount of CH1 required to give 50% dissociation, with an inhibition constant Ki = 0.51 ± 0.01 μM.
evidence: Calculated from dose-response data shown in Figure 2.

claim: IRE1 LD interacts with the BiP ATPase domain to produce 100% FRET signal equivalent to that produced by full-length BiP.
source: We observed a 100% FRET signal equivalent to that resulting from full-length YFP-BiP interaction with CFP-IRE1 LD, whereas we measured no FRET signal when using the SBD (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: No FRET signal was measured when using the BiP SBD with IRE1 LD.
source: We observed a 100% FRET signal equivalent to that resulting from full-length YFP-BiP interaction with CFP-IRE1 LD, whereas we measured no FRET signal when using the SBD (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: The ATPase domain of BiP is necessary for the interaction with IRE1 LD.
source: This reaffirms the notion that the ATPase domain of BiP is necessary for the interaction with IRE1 LD, consistent with microscale thermophoresis (MST) and pull-down assay measurements (Carrara et al., 2015); furthermore, this interaction has also been suggested by another study (Todd-Corlett et al., 2007).
evidence: Interpretation of data from Figure 3B-C, supported by prior studies.

claim: The addition of 5 mM ATP, ADP and AMP-PNP to CFP-IRE1 LD and YFP-BiP did not have a significant impact upon the FRET signal.
source: We added 5 mM ATP, ADP and AMP-PNP to CFP-IRE1 LD and YFP-BiP, and compared these to samples examined in the absence of nucleotide. We observed no significant difference upon the addition of various nucleotides, or in the absence of nucleotide, with all samples measuring almost 100% FRET signal (Figure 3D).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 3D.

claim: IRE1 LD–BiP association is independent of nucleotide binding.
source: This result again suggests that IRE1 LD–BiP association is independent of nucleotide binding.
evidence: Interpretation of nucleotide addition experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The addition of folded antitrypsin, RNase A, and apolipoprotein had no affect on the FRET signal, with all three measurements close to or equal to 100%.
source: The addition of folded antitrypsin, RNase A, and apolipoprotein had no affect on the FRET signal, with all three measurements close to or equal to 100% (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Experimental measurements shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The addition of misfolded versions of antitrypsin, RNase A, and apolipoprotein reduced the FRET signal to approximately 6%.
source: The addition of misfolded versions of the same ER proteins: antitrypsin, RNase A, and apolipoprotein, reduced the signal to ~6% (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Experimental measurements shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: For TTRD18G, which lacked a folded control, the FRET signal was reduced to approximately 2%.
source: For TTRD18G, which lacked a folded control, the FRET signal was reduced to ~2% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only the misfolded state of the ER proteins induce an effect by binding to canonical BiP SBD, resulting in IRE1 and BiP dissociation via the ATPase domain, with resultant loss in FRET signal.
source: First, the data clearly indicate that only the misfolded state of the ER proteins induce an effect, by binding to canonical BiP SBD, resulting in IRE1 and BiP dissociation via the ATPase domain, with resultant loss in FRET signal.
evidence: Interpretation of data from Figure 4A-C comparing folded and misfolded proteins.

claim: Dissociation of IRE1 and BiP upon binding of misfolded protein is not specific to CH1 substrate.
source: Second, dissociation of IRE1 and BiP upon binding of misfolded protein is not specific to CH1 substrate, rather other ER misfolded proteins can induce dissociation by binding to BiP SBD, consistent with BiP being a HSP70-type chaperone.
evidence: Interpretation of data from Figure 4 showing multiple misfolded proteins cause dissociation.

claim: Other ER misfolded proteins can induce dissociation by binding to BiP SBD, consistent with BiP being a HSP70-type chaperone.
source: Second, dissociation of IRE1 and BiP upon binding of misfolded protein is not specific to CH1 substrate, rather other ER misfolded proteins can induce dissociation by binding to BiP SBD, consistent with BiP being a HSP70-type chaperone.
evidence: Interpretation of data from Figure 4 in context of BiP's known function.

claim: V461F is a key mutation of BiP that prevents misfolded substrate engagement.
source: V461F is a key mutation of BiP that prevents misfolded substrate engagement (Laufen et al., 1999; Petrova et al., 2008); it does this by inserting a bulky side chain that sterically hinders access to the active site of the SBD.
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The V461F mutation prevents misfolded substrate engagement by inserting a bulky side chain that sterically hinders access to the active site of the SBD.
source: V461F is a key mutation of BiP that prevents misfolded substrate engagement (Laufen et al., 1999; Petrova et al., 2008); it does this by inserting a bulky side chain that sterically hinders access to the active site of the SBD.
evidence: Mechanistic explanation from cited literature.

claim: For YFP-BiPWT, a 95% reduction in the FRET signal was observed upon addition of misfolded protein.
source: For YFP-BiPWT, we observed a 95% reduction in the FRET signal upon addition of misfolded protein.
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The addition of misfolded protein to the YFP-BiPV461F sample showed no significant loss in FRET signal.
source: By contrast, the addition of misfolded protein to the YFP-BiPV461F sample showed no significant loss in FRET signal (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: In the presence of 5 mM ATP, both BiPWT and BiPT229A interacted with CFP-IRE1 LD.
source: In the presence of 5 mM ATP, both BiPWT and BiPT229A interacted with CFP-IRE1 LD; moreover, dissociation of complex was caused by addition of misfolded protein in a manner that was independent of ATP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dissociation of the BiP-IRE1 complex was caused by addition of misfolded protein in a manner that was independent of ATP.
source: In the presence of 5 mM ATP, both BiPWT and BiPT229A interacted with CFP-IRE1 LD; moreover, dissociation of complex was caused by addition of misfolded protein in a manner that was independent of ATP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The double mutant BiPV461F, T229A associated with CFP-IRE1 LD in the presence of ATP, but failed to dissociate upon the addition of misfolded protein.
source: However, the double mutant, BiPV461F, T229A, associated with CFP-IRE1 LD in the presence of ATP, but failed to dissociate upon the addition of misfolded protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The double mutant BiPV461F, T229A behaved in exactly the same way as the SBD single mutant BiPV461F.
source: Thus this mutant behaved in exactly the same way as the SBD single mutant, BiPV461F (Figure 5A–C), indicating again that the BiP–IRE1 association and dissociation were independent of nucleotides.
evidence: Comparison of experimental results from Figure 5.

claim: The BiP–IRE1 association and dissociation were independent of nucleotides.
source: Thus this mutant behaved in exactly the same way as the SBD single mutant, BiPV461F (Figure 5A–C), indicating again that the BiP–IRE1 association and dissociation were independent of nucleotides.
evidence: Interpretation of mutant data from Figure 5.

claim: In the absence of ER stress, an interaction was observed both between IRE1 and BiP wildtype and between IRE1 and BiP V461F.
source: In the absence of ER stress, we observed an interaction both between IRE1 and BiP wildtype and between IRE1 and BiP V461F.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Upon addition of ER stress, the interaction between IRE1 and BiP wildtype was significantly reduced.
source: Upon addition of ER stress, however, the interaction between IRE1 and BiP wildtype was significantly reduced, whereas no loss in interaction was observed with BiP V461F, thus supporting the in vitro FRET data.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No loss in interaction was observed between IRE1 and BiP V461F upon addition of ER stress.
source: Upon addition of ER stress, however, the interaction between IRE1 and BiP wildtype was significantly reduced, whereas no loss in interaction was observed with BiP V461F, thus supporting the in vitro FRET data.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: When BiP forms an interaction with the IRE1 LD via its ATPase domain, misfolded proteins can bind to the canonical active site of the BiP SBD to cause dissociation of BiP, resulting in loss of FRET signal.
source: Taken together, both the in vitro and cellular data indicate that when BiP forms an interaction with the IRE1 LD, via its ATPase domain, misfolded proteins can bind to the canonical active site of the BiP SBD to cause dissociation of BiP, resulting in loss of FRET signal.
evidence: Summary interpretation of data from Figures 1-5.

claim: The BiPV461F mutant, in which access to the active site is blocked, was unable to interact with misfolded protein and hence could not effect the dissociation of BiP from IRE1, resulting in no reduction of FRET signal.
source: The BiPV461F mutant, in which access to the active site is blocked, was unable to interact with misfolded protein and hence could not effect the dissociation of BiP from IRE1, resulting in no reduction of FRET signal.
evidence: Interpretation of BiPV461F mutant data from Figure 5.

claim: As misfolded protein binding to the BiP substrate-binding site caused BiP ATPase domain to dissociate from IRE1, an allosteric mechanism is clearly suggested.
source: Moreover, as misfolded protein binding to the BiP substrate-binding site caused BiP ATPase domain to dissociate from IRE1, an allosteric mechanism is clearly suggested, supporting our model.
evidence: Interpretation of the overall experimental findings.

claim: An in vitro FRET UPR induction assay was developed that quantifies the association and dissociation of the IRE1 LD from BiP upon ER stress.
source: In the present study, we have developed an in vitro FRET UPR induction assay that quantifies the association and dissociation of the IRE1 LD from BiP upon ER stress; thereby, describing an important technical tool for dissecting the UPR induction mechanism that measures a three-component interacting system.
evidence: Summary of the study's main methodological contribution.

claim: The FRET assay describes an important technical tool for dissecting the UPR induction mechanism that measures a three-component interacting system.
source: In the present study, we have developed an in vitro FRET UPR induction assay that quantifies the association and dissociation of the IRE1 LD from BiP upon ER stress; thereby, describing an important technical tool for dissecting the UPR induction mechanism that measures a three-component interacting system.
evidence: Interpretation of the significance of the developed assay.

claim: Misfolded proteins are being recognized or sensed by the BiP SBD when interacting with the IRE1 LD.
source: The mutant data, along with the observation that ER misfolded proteins (and not the same proteins in their native folded state) cause dissociation, clearly indicates that misfolded proteins are being recognized or sensed by the BiP SBD when interacting with the IRE1 LD.
evidence: Interpretation of the combined mutant and folded/misfolded protein data.

claim: The present data provide evidence that would discount a BiP competition model.
source: Interestingly, the present data provide evidence that would discount a BiP competition model (Bertolotti et al., 2000; Kimata et al., 2003; Okamura et al., 2000; Liu et al., 2000).
evidence: Interpretation of the study's findings in relation to alternative models.

claim: In the BiP competition model, IRE1 binds to BiP via the SBD, which is the same site that misfolded proteins bind to BiP.
source: In this model, IRE1 binds to BiP via the SBD, which is the same site that misfolded proteins bind to BiP.
evidence: Description of the alternative competition model from cited literature.

claim: In the BiP competition model, upon ER stress, misfolded protein titre BiP off from IRE1 in a competitive fashion, resulting in dimerization and activation of UPR.
source: Upon ER stress, misfolded protein titre BiP off from IRE1 in a competitive fashion, resulting in dimerization and activation of UPR.
evidence: Description of the alternative competition model from cited literature.

claim: In the BiP competition model, the dissociation process is ATP dependent.
source: This process is ATP dependent (Bertolotti et al., 2000; Kimata et al., 2003), with ATP (and not necessarily misfolded proteins) being sufficient to cause dissociation of IRE1 and BiP.
evidence: Description of the alternative competition model from cited literature.

claim: In the BiP competition model, ATP (and not necessarily misfolded proteins) is sufficient to cause dissociation of IRE1 and BiP.
source: This process is ATP dependent (Bertolotti et al., 2000; Kimata et al., 2003), with ATP (and not necessarily misfolded proteins) being sufficient to cause dissociation of IRE1 and BiP.
evidence: Description of the alternative competition model from cited literature.

claim: The interaction between IRE1 and BiP occurs via the ATPase domain of BiP and is independent of nucleotides.
source: Our in vitro data support an allosteric model (Carrara et al., 2015); whereby, the interaction between IRE1 and BiP occurs via the ATPase domain of BiP and is independent of nucleotides; this clearly indicates a UPR signaling productive association and not a chaperone-substrate type interaction.
evidence: Summary of the study's findings supporting the allosteric model.

claim: The interaction between IRE1 and BiP via the ATPase domain indicates a UPR signaling productive association and not a chaperone-substrate type interaction.
source: Our in vitro data support an allosteric model (Carrara et al., 2015); whereby, the interaction between IRE1 and BiP occurs via the ATPase domain of BiP and is independent of nucleotides; this clearly indicates a UPR signaling productive association and not a chaperone-substrate type interaction.
evidence: Interpretation of the mechanistic implications of the findings.

claim: As binding between IRE1 and BiP, and the detection of misfolded proteins, involves two different domains of BiP that are coupled by conformational change, there is no requirement for the association with IRE1 and detection of misfolded protein to be a competitive process.
source: Moreover, as binding between IRE1 and BiP, and the detection of misfolded proteins, involves two different domains of BiP that are coupled by conformational change, there is no requirement for the association with IRE1 and detection of misfolded protein to be a competitive process, thus reconciling the sensitive nature of UPR signaling.
evidence: Logical inference from the allosteric mechanism.

claim: The allosteric mechanism reconciles the sensitive nature of UPR signaling.
source: Moreover, as binding between IRE1 and BiP, and the detection of misfolded proteins, involves two different domains of BiP that are coupled by conformational change, there is no requirement for the association with IRE1 and detection of misfolded protein to be a competitive process, thus reconciling the sensitive nature of UPR signaling.
evidence: Interpretation of the biological significance of the allosteric mechanism.

claim: The binding and release of BiP from IRE1 is independent of ATPase activity.
source: Although our model indicates that the binding and release of BiP from IRE1 is independent of ATPase activity, it could be that nucleotides have influence over other aspects of UPR signaling.
evidence: Summary of the study's findings regarding nucleotide independence.

claim: Nucleotides greatly impact BiP conformation, with ADP-bound BiP adopting a substantially different conformation to that of ATP-bound BiP.
source: It is known that nucleotides greatly impact BiP conformation, with ADP-bound BiP adopting a substantially different conformation to that of ATP-bound BiP.
evidence: Established knowledge about BiP conformational states.

claim: The results of the current study are consistent with previous data from microscale thermophoresis (MST) and pull-down assays that have shown an interaction between the ATPase domain (and not the SBD) of BiP and IRE1.
source: The results of the current study are also consistent with our previous data from microscale thermophoresis (MST) and pull-down assays that have shown an interaction between the ATPase domain (and not the SBD) of BiP and IRE1; this observation has been reported before (Todd-Corlett et al., 2007).
evidence: Comparison with prior experimental findings.

claim: The interaction between the ATPase domain of BiP and IRE1 has been reported by Todd-Corlett et al., 2007.
source: The results of the current study are also consistent with our previous data from microscale thermophoresis (MST) and pull-down assays that have shown an interaction between the ATPase domain (and not the SBD) of BiP and IRE1; this observation has been reported before (Todd-Corlett et al., 2007).
evidence: Citation to independent prior study.

claim: The data enhance the experimental evidence suggesting an allosteric mechanism for UPR induction.
source: Furthermore, the data enhance the experimental evidence suggesting an allosteric mechanism for UPR induction.
evidence: Summary of the study's contribution to understanding UPR mechanism.

claim: Fluorescent fusion constructs were designed in which CFP and YFP were attached N-terminally to human IRE1 LD (32-440) and human BiP (28-654), respectively, via a short 15aa linker (GGAGGAGGAGGAGGA).
source: Fluorescent fusion constructs were designed in which the fluorescent proteins CFP and YFP were attached N-terminally to human IRE1 LD (32-440) and human BiP (28-654), respectively, via a short 15aa linker (GGAGGAGGAGGAGGA).
evidence: Description of construct design in Materials and methods.

claim: The fluorescent fusion constructs were cloned into a pGEX 6p1 vector, containing a GST tag and a PreScission protease site.
source: This construct was then cloned into a pGEX 6p1 vector, containing a GST tag and a PreScission protease site, and expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) cells (Agilent, CA, USA).
evidence: Description of cloning strategy in Materials and methods.

claim: The fluorescent fusion constructs were expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) cells.
source: This construct was then cloned into a pGEX 6p1 vector, containing a GST tag and a PreScission protease site, and expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) cells (Agilent, CA, USA).
evidence: Description of expression system in Materials and methods.

claim: FRET assay experiments were carried out using a CLARIOstar microplate reader.
source: FRET assay experiments were carried out using a CLARIOstar microplate reader (BMG Labtech, DE).
evidence: Description of instrumentation in Materials and methods.

claim: Fluorescently labelled proteins were combined in an equimolar ratio in all samples.
source: Fluorescently labelled proteins were combined in an equimolar ratio in all samples.
evidence: Description of experimental protocol in Materials and methods.

claim: Folded or misfolded protein was added at 10-fold molar excess to the concentration of the fluorescent proteins, unless the concentration is otherwise specified.
source: Folded or misfolded protein was added at 10-fold molar excess to the concentration of the fluorescent proteins, unless the concentration is otherwise specified.
evidence: Description of experimental protocol in Materials and methods.

claim: The concentration for each of the fluorescent proteins was adjusted to 30 μM in a volume of 160 μL.
source: The mixture was then diluted with buffer C to a volume of 160 μL, adjusting the concentration for each of the fluorescent proteins to 30 μM.
evidence: Description of experimental protocol in Materials and methods.

claim: Suspension Human Embryonic Kidney cells (Expi293F) were cultured in serum-free Gibco's Expi293 Expression medium.
source: Suspension Human Embryonic Kidney cells (Expi293F) were cultured in serum-free Gibco's Expi293 Expression medium.
evidence: Description of cell culture conditions in Materials and methods.

claim: DNA containing Flag-IRE1 and either HA-BiP WT or HA-BiPV461F were co-transfected with ExpiFectamine reagent to a concentration of 15 μg total DNA (1 ug/ml DNA).
source: DNA containing Flag-IRE1 and either HA-BiP WT or HA-BiPV461F (which were present in pcDNA 3.1(+) vector) were co-transfected with ExpiFectamine reagent to a concentration of 15 μg total DNA (1 ug/ml DNA) (ThermoFisher), according to the manufacturer's protocol (ThermoFisher).
evidence: Description of transfection protocol in Materials and methods.

claim: After 48 hr, cells were either harvested or 5 μM tunicamycin was added for 2 hr to produce ER-stressed samples.
source: After 48 hr, cells were either harvested or 5 μM tunicamycin was added for 2 hr to produce ER-stressed samples.
evidence: Description of ER stress induction protocol in Materials and methods.

claim: FRET occurs when two fluorophores are in close proximity, approximately 1–10 nm distance.
source: If YFP is in close proximity, approximately 1–10 nm distance (Bajar et al., 2016), then energy transfer will occur between CFP and YFP, resulting in an emission peak at 530 nm wavelength.
evidence: Established principle of FRET from cited literature.

claim: Ratio-metric measurement produces less noise than individual fluorescent intensity observations and is a more reliable FRET signal measure.
source: This ratio-metric measurement produces less noise then individual fluorescent intensity observations, and is a more reliable FRET signal measure (Bajar et al., 2016; Pollok and Heim, 1999; Martin et al., 2008).
evidence: Established methodological principle from cited literature.

claim: CFP contributes a significant fluorescence emission intensity at 530 nm (also referred to as CFP leakage) when excited at 430 nm.
source: The negative controls measure a FRET ratio of ~0.34 due to CFP, which contributes a significant fluorescence emission intensity at 530 nm (also referred to as CFP leakage) when excited at 430 nm.
